Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Container default credential leak — PKP_DB_PASSWORD=changeMePlease and --secret
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Web service in container spawning interactive shell (Redis/nginx RCE) · [LLM] Container privilege escalation via Looney Tunables, PwnKit, sudo chroot · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] perfctl rootkit — /etc/ld.so.preload write or LD_PRELOAD on root daemon · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Article-specific behavioural hunt — What’s in the container? Analyzing vulnerabilities, risks and protection with Ka
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Container egress to cryptominer pool / Kinsing C2
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Container-to-container horizontal scan — Dero miner self-propagation
[LLM] Web service in container spawning interactive shell (Redis/nginx RCE) Exploitation High
Hunts CVE-2025-49844 (Redis Lua RCE) and CVE-2026-24061 (nginx) post-exploitation pattern: redis-server, nginx, node or java spawning sh/bash/busybox inside a containerised host — the unambiguous fingerprint of RCE landing inside a vulnerable image. Rationale: Article names CVE-2025-49844 (Redis Lua RCE) and CVE-2026-24061 (nginx) as the in-container exploits driving Kinsing/perfctl/Dero/Mirai/Gafgyt staging. Cross-checked against MITRE T1190 page and abuse.ch ThreatFox notes on Kinsing post-exploit shell drop patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/win.kinsing/
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("redis-server","nginx","node","java","httpd","apache2","php-fpm")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","busybox","ash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","/tmp/","/dev/shm/","chmod +x","base64 -d","bash -i","|sh","|bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("redis-server","nginx","node","java","httpd","apache2","php-fpm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/busybox","/ash","/zsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","/tmp/","/dev/shm/","chmod +x","base64 -d","bash -i","|sh","|bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Container Web Service Spawning Interactive Shell
id: 7e1b8b22-7c11-4f2d-9b40-9a5a3e7e1a01
description: Detects redis-server, nginx, node, java, httpd or apache2 spawning sh/bash with download or staging command-line — classic post-exploit pattern for CVE-2025-49844 / CVE-2026-24061 inside containers.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/container-security-typical-issues/119974/
author: SOC
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/redis-server'
      - '/nginx'
      - '/node'
      - '/java'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/php-fpm'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/busybox'
      - '/ash'
      - '/zsh'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'curl '
      - 'wget '
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - 'chmod +x'
      - 'base64 -d'
      - 'bash -i'
      - '|sh'
      - '|bash'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:(linux.auditd OR windows.sysmon) @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.parent.name:(redis-server OR nginx OR node OR java OR httpd OR apache2 OR php-fpm) OR @ParentImage:(*\\redis-server* OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\java.exe)) @process.command_line:(*curl* OR *wget* OR *"/tmp/"* OR *"/dev/shm/"* OR *"chmod +x"* OR *"base64 -d"* OR *"bash -i"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(redis-server|nginx|node|java|httpd|apache2|php-fpm)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|busybox|ash|zsh)$/i
| regex("(curl |wget |/tmp/|/dev/shm/|chmod \\+x|base64 -d|bash -i|\\|sh|\\|bash)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("redis-server","nginx","node","java","httpd","apache2") Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","busybox","ash") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)(curl|wget|chmod|/tmp/|/dev/shm/|base64|nc |bash -i)") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("redis-server","nginx","node","java","httpd","apache2") Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","busybox","ash") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)(curl|wget|chmod|/tmp/|/dev/shm/|base64|nc |bash -i)") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
[LLM] Container privilege escalation via Looney Tunables, PwnKit, sudo chroot Exploitation High
Detects CVE-2023-4911 (GLIBC_TUNABLES env-var corruption), CVE-2021-4034 (pkexec PwnKit) and CVE-2025-32463 (sudo --chroot/-R) — the exact local-root chain named in the article for Kinsing and perfctl campaigns. Rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2023-4911 (Looney Tunables, Kinsing), CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit, perfctl) and CVE-2025-32463 (sudo). Detection anchors on the unique exploit signatures — GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc. prefix is the Looney Tunables hallmark, sudo --chroot/-R is CVE-2025-32463-specific. Cross-checked against Qualys advisory for Looney Tunables and the sudo CVE-2025-32463 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2023/10/03/cve-2023-4911-looney-tunables-local-privilege-escalation-in-the-glibcs-ld-so • https://www.stratascale.com/vulnerability-alert-CVE-2025-32463-sudo-chroot • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1180/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.")
    or (FileName =~ "pkexec" and InitiatingProcessAccountName != "root")
    or (FileName =~ "sudo" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--chroot "," -R /","--chroot="," -R="))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.")
    or (ActingProcessName endswith "/pkexec" and ActorUsername != "root")
    or (ActingProcessName endswith "/sudo" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--chroot "," -R /","--chroot="," -R="))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Linux Local Privilege Escalation via Looney Tunables, PwnKit or sudo chroot
id: 4d3b9c2e-2f01-4a8e-b6ed-3e6f1e2c2b02
description: Detects the three local-root chains named in the Kaspersky container-security article — CVE-2023-4911 GLIBC_TUNABLES, CVE-2021-4034 pkexec PwnKit, CVE-2025-32463 sudo --chroot/-R.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/container-security-typical-issues/119974/
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-4911
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-4034
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-32463
author: SOC
date: 2026/05/29
tags:

  - attack.t1548.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  sel_tunables:
    CommandLine|contains: 'GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.'
  sel_pkexec:
    Image|endswith: '/pkexec'
  sel_sudo:
    Image|endswith: '/sudo'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--chroot '
      - ' -R /'
      - '--chroot='
  condition: sel_tunables or sel_pkexec or sel_sudo
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@process.command_line:*GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.* OR (@process.executable.path:*/pkexec AND -@user.name:root) OR (@process.executable.path:*/sudo AND @process.command_line:(*"--chroot "* OR *" -R /"*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (CommandLine=/GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc\./
   OR (ImageFileName=/\/pkexec$/i AND UserName!="root")
   OR (ImageFileName=/\/sudo$/i AND CommandLine=/(--chroot |\s-R\s+\/|--chroot=)/))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process IN ("*GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.*","*pkexec*","*sudo --chroot*","*sudo -R *") OR Processes.process_name="pkexec") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process IN ("*GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.*","*pkexec*","*sudo --chroot*","*sudo -R *") OR Processes.process_name="pkexec") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
[LLM] perfctl rootkit — /etc/ld.so.preload write or LD_PRELOAD on root daemon Installation High
Hunts the perfctl userland rootkit footprint named in the article: write to /etc/ld.so.preload, or a long-running root daemon launched with LD_PRELOAD pointing at a non-standard library — both are the canonical Linux process-hiding persistence pattern. Rationale: Article explicitly states perfctl 'install a rootkit that hides the presence of perfctl on the system' after CVE-2021-4034. /etc/ld.so.preload and LD_PRELOAD are the canonical Linux userland rootkit primitives. Cross-checked against Aqua Nautilus perfctl write-up and MITRE T1574.006 page. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/perfctl-a-stealthy-malware-targeting-millions-of-linux-servers/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/006/
ATT&CKT1014 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
union
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where FolderPath =~ "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
),
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "LD_PRELOAD="
  | where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/","LD_PRELOAD=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="LD_PRELOAD_exec", FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName
)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(
  ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where TargetFilePath =~ "/etc/ld.so.preload"
  | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
),
(
  ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "LD_PRELOAD="
  | where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/","LD_PRELOAD=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/"))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=DvcHostname, ActorUsername=ActorUsername, EventType="LD_PRELOAD_exec", TargetFilePath="", ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Write to /etc/ld.so.preload or Suspicious LD_PRELOAD on Root Daemon

[LLM] Container default credential leak — PKP_DB_PASSWORD=changeMePlease and --secret Weaponization Medium
Hunts the exact plaintext credential anti-patterns shown in the article's Dockerfile screenshots: PKP_DB_PASSWORD set to changeMePlease (or any default vendor value) baked into image layers, and processes launched with --secret <value> arguments visible in /proc. Rationale: Article's verbatim code blocks include PKP_DB_PASSWORD, changeMePlease and --secret as plaintext-credential examples (Block 1/2/3 in tables). The Phase 3 citation explicitly calls out passwords-on-command-line being visible in /proc. PKP_DB_PASSWORD is the documented OJS/PKP default — confirmed via PKP project docs. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.pkp.sfu.ca/admin-guide/en/deploy-docker • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.003 T1078.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PKP_DB_PASSWORD=","=changeMePlease"," --secret ","MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=","POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres","REDIS_PASSWORD=redis")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vault","sops","kubectl"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PKP_DB_PASSWORD=","=changeMePlease"," --secret ","MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=","POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres","REDIS_PASSWORD=redis")
| where not (ParentProcessName has_any ("vault","sops","kubectl"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Container-to-container horizontal scan — Dero miner self-propagation Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects compromised containers fanning out to scan adjacent network ranges for additional vulnerable services, the article-described Dero miner self-propagation behaviour. Threshold-based: many unique destinations on a small set of vulnerable-service ports within a short window, sourced from a single container IP. Rationale: Article's Phase 6 citation describes Dero miner self-propagation via infected containers scanning for new targets. Port set chosen for the article-referenced vulnerable services: Redis (6379, CVE-2025-49844), Docker API (2375/2376), nginx-fronted apps (8080/9000), etcd (2379), DBs. cloudwatch_query left empty — container-to-container traffic does not naturally land in CloudWatch CloudTrail/VPC-flow trails in the analyst-pivot shape this UC needs. Cross-checked against Wiz Dero campaign write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/dero-miner-attacks-on-kubernetes-clusters • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1046/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionAttempt" or ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemotePort in (22, 2375, 2376, 6379, 8080, 9000, 9200, 2379, 5432, 3306)
| where RemoteIPType in ("Private","Public")
| summarize UniqueDests = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, LocalIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where UniqueDests > 50
| order by UniqueDests desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DstPortNumber in (22, 2375, 2376, 6379, 8080, 9000, 9200, 2379, 5432, 3306)
| summarize UniqueDests = dcount(DstIpAddr), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber, 10)
          by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where UniqueDests > 50
| order by UniqueDests desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @network.destination.port:(22 OR 2375 OR 2376 OR 6379 OR 8080 OR 9000 OR 9200 OR 2379 OR 5432 OR 3306)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemotePort=22 OR RemotePort=2375 OR RemotePort=2376 OR RemotePort=6379 OR RemotePort=8080 OR RemotePort=9000 OR RemotePort=9200 OR RemotePort=2379 OR RemotePort=5432 OR RemotePort=3306
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=UniqueDests))
| UniqueDests > 50
CLOUD

| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(All_Traffic.dest) as unique_dests min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,2375,2376,6379,8080,9000,9200,2379,5432,3306) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where unique_dests > 50 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.dest) as unique_dests min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,2375,2376,6379,8080,9000,9200,2379,5432,3306) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where unique_dests > 50 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
[LLM] Container egress to cryptominer pool / Kinsing C2 Command & Control High
Detects post-compromise C2 from containers: outbound connections to Stratum mining-pool ports (3333/4444/5555/7777/14444) or to known Kinsing/perfctl/Dero infrastructure indicators, initiated from a container-resident process (curl/wget/xmrig/perfctl). Rationale: Article ties Kinsing/perfctl/Dero/Mirai/Gafgyt to compromised containers (Phase 8). Stratum port set is the documented mining-pool default for Monero/Dero. Domain indicators cross-checked against abuse.ch ThreatFox Kinsing entries and Aqua Nautilus perfctl/Dero write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/win.kinsing/ • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/perfctl-a-stealthy-malware-targeting-millions-of-linux-servers/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/dero-miner-attacks-on-kubernetes-clusters
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1496
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
union
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
  | where RemotePort in (3333, 4444, 5555, 7777, 14444, 14433, 45700)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Signal="stratum_port"
),
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("xmrig","kinsing","perfctl","derohe.org","dero-stratum","minexmr","supportxmr","nanopool","pool.minexmr")

)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(
  ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
  | where DstPortNumber in (3333, 4444, 5555, 7777, 14444, 14433, 45700)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, Signal="stratum_port"
),

)

Malicious RVTools Installer Abuses Sectigo Certificate to Bypass SmartScreen Warnings

Cyber Security News
2026-05-29 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A trusted tool for VMware administrators has been weaponized. Attackers built a fake version of RVTools, a widely used utility for managing virtual infrastructure, and disguised it with a real digital certificate to slip past Windows security warnings without raising a flag. RVTools is a staple in enterprise environments. IT administrators rely on it daily [&#8230;] The post Malicious RVTools Installer Abuses Sectigo Certificate to Bypass SmartScreen Warnings appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious RVTools MSI signed by Xiamen Lunwei Huage (Sectigo) — hash + cert subject · [LLM] PowerShell download of winp.zip ~33MB from Dropbox into %APPDATA% · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] msiexec spawning wscript Binary.MyScript.vbs → hidden powershell (RVTools chain) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malicious RVTools Installer Abuses Sectigo Certificate to Bypass SmartScreen War
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RVTools RAT persistence: Run key + SYSTEM scheduled task pointing to AppData python · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Portable python.exe launching from AppData running Pmanager.py / collector.py · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Malicious RVTools MSI signed by Xiamen Lunwei Huage (Sectigo) — hash + cert subject Delivery High
Hunts the trojanized RVTools.msi installer by the K7-published file hashes and by the fraudulent Sectigo code-signing subject 'Xiamen Lunwei Huage Network Co., Ltd.' Catches the artifact at landing (download) or at execution even after the cert is revoked, including renamed/repacked variants that re-use the same Authenticode subject. Rationale: Uses the K7-published SHA256/MD5 hashes for the MSI, VBS, and both Python modules, the 'Xiamen Lunwei Huage' Sectigo signing subject (revoked but still present in cached/dropped binaries), and an RVTools-named msiexec invocation as a backstop. Hashes are second-sourced by the broader RVTools-installer attack chain reporting on malware.news and Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/rvtools-masquerade-how-a-signed-fake-installer-deploys-a-modular-python-rat/107384 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/05/19/rvtools-installer-malware/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/05/rvtools-official-site-hacked-to-deliver.html
ATT&CKT1588.003 T1036.001 T1204.002

        or MD5 in~ ("64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b","01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc","71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362","9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileOriginUrl),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (FileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("RVTools","rvtools"))
        or SHA256 == "d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4"
        or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Xiamen Lunwei Huage"

[LLM] msiexec spawning wscript Binary.MyScript.vbs → hidden powershell (RVTools chain) Exploitation High
Catches the second-stage execution: the signed MSI invokes wscript.exe against the embedded Binary.MyScript.vbs from its binary table, which uses decimal-to-character encoding to launch a hidden PowerShell. The parent=msiexec, child=wscript on a VBS named Binary.MyScript with a PowerShell grandchild is the article-specific tree. Rationale: Pins on the article-specific filename 'Binary.MyScript.vbs' (the MSI binary-table entry) and the msiexec→wscript→powershell tree, plus the decimal-to-char encoding signature `[char]\d{2,3}` mentioned in the K7 write-up. Time-window join keeps FPs low — legitimate MSIs almost never spawn wscript→powershell. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/rvtools-masquerade-how-a-signed-fake-installer-deploys-a-modular-python-rat/107384
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1059.005 T1059.001 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let VbsExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
    | where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Binary.MyScript.vbs","MyScript.vbs")
    | project VbsTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, VbsPid=ProcessId, VbsCmd=ProcessCommandLine, DeviceName, AccountName;
let PsChild = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
    | where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-w hidden","-WindowStyle Hidden","-WindowStyle h","-nop","-noprofile","DownloadFile","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","dropbox")
        or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\[char\]\d{2,3}"
    | project PsTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, VbsPid=InitiatingProcessId, PsCmd=ProcessCommandLine;
VbsExec
| join kind=inner PsChild on DeviceId, VbsPid
| where PsTime between (VbsTime .. VbsTime + 5m)
| project VbsTime, DeviceName, AccountName, VbsCmd, PsTime, PsCmd
let VbsExec = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

    | where TargetProcessName endswith_cs "wscript.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith_cs "cscript.exe"
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("Binary.MyScript.vbs","MyScript.vbs")
    | project VbsTime=TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, VbsPid=TargetProcessId, VbsCmd=TargetProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername;
let PsChild = ImProcessCreate

[LLM] PowerShell download of winp.zip ~33MB from Dropbox into %APPDATA% Delivery High
Detects the third stage: a hidden PowerShell pulls a ~33MB archive named winp.zip from a Dropbox URL and extracts it into the AppData folder. Targets the specific filename plus the Dropbox-origin + AppData-destination combination — distinctive even without the original IPs. Rationale: Article specifies the exact archive name 'winp.zip', size ~33MB, Dropbox CDN origin, and AppData drop path. The combined PowerShell→Dropbox→AppData\winp.zip chain is unique enough that file-name alone is high-fidelity; the Dropbox correlation in the join further suppresses any unrelated user-saved zips. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/rvtools-masquerade-how-a-signed-fake-installer-deploys-a-modular-python-rat/107384
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let DropboxDownload = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("dropbox.com","dl.dropboxusercontent.com","www.dropbox.com")
    | project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
let ZipDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "winp.zip" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^winp.*\.zip$"
    | where FolderPath has @"\AppData\"
    | project FileTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union DropboxDownload, ZipDrop
| summarize NetEvents=countif(isnotempty(RemoteUrl)), FileEvents=countif(isnotempty(FileName)),
            arg_max(NetTime, RemoteUrl), arg_max(FileTime, FolderPath, FileSize)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId
| where NetEvents > 0 and FileEvents > 0
let Dropbox = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Url has_any ("dropbox.com","dl.dropboxusercontent.com")
    | where SrcUsername != "" 
    | project NetTime=TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, FileName;
let ZipDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^winp.*\.zip$"
    | where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\"
    | project FileTime=TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine;
ZipDrop
| join kind=leftouter Dropbox on Computer
| where NetTime between (FileTime - 10m .. FileTime)
| project FileTime, Computer, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, Url, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by FileTime desc

[LLM] Portable python.exe launching from AppData running Pmanager.py / collector.py Command & Control High
Hunts the post-reboot RAT stage: a Python interpreter executing from the user's AppData (part of the portable Python bundle dropped via winp.zip) launching the Pmanager.py C2 module or the collector.py recon module, optionally with configA.json output in %TEMP%. The combination of AppData-resident python + the two named scripts is article-specific. Rationale: Article names the two Python modules verbatim (Pmanager.py, collector.py), the output file (configA.json), the AppData install path, and the 300-second beacon cadence. Filename + AppData-resident python.exe is high-fidelity; the network sub-query layers in the ~5-minute beacon interval. No second sourcing needed for filenames — they are unique strings. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/rvtools-masquerade-how-a-signed-fake-installer-deploys-a-modular-python-rat/107384
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1071.001 T1041 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let PyExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "python.exe" or FileName =~ "pythonw.exe"
    | where FolderPath has @"\AppData\"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Pmanager.py","collector.py","configA.json")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let Beacons = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\"
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize Connections=count(), DistinctRemotes=dcount(RemoteIP), FirstBeacon=min(Timestamp), LastBeacon=max(Timestamp)
              by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
    | where Connections >= 3 and (datetime_diff('second', LastBeacon, FirstBeacon) / Connections) between (240 .. 360);
PyExec
| union Beacons
| order by Timestamp desc
let PyExec = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetProcessName endswith_cs "python.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith_cs "pythonw.exe"
    | where TargetProcessName has @"\AppData\"
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("Pmanager.py","collector.py","configA.json")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessId;
let Beacons = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where SrcUsername has @"\AppData\" or DstHostname != ""
    | where SrcUsername != ""
    | summarize Connections=count(), DistinctRemotes=dcount(DstIpAddr), FirstBeacon=min(TimeGenerated), LastBeacon=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer=DvcHostname, SrcUsername
    | where Connections >= 3 and (datetime_diff('second', LastBeacon, FirstBeacon) / Connections) between (240 .. 360);
PyExec
| join kind=leftouter Beacons on Computer
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\AppData\*\python.exe OR *\AppData\*\pythonw.exe OR *\AppData\*\PYTHON.EXE) @CommandLine:(*Pmanager.py* OR *collector.py* OR *configA.json*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\AppData\\.*\\python(w)?\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(Pmanager\.py|collector\.py|configA\.json)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

[LLM] RVTools RAT persistence: Run key + SYSTEM scheduled task pointing to AppData python Installation High
Catches the persistence install: a Registry Run value or a Scheduled Task running as SYSTEM whose command references python.exe under AppData and/or Pmanager.py. Either artifact alone is high-signal because legitimate apps almost never persist a portable Python interpreter from an AppData path under SYSTEM context. Rationale: Article specifies persistence is achieved through both a Registry Run entry and a SYSTEM-level scheduled task — uncommon combo for a user-mode portable Python install. The value/command must reference the article's filenames (Pmanager.py / collector.py) or python under AppData; both predicates together are very high signal. The SYSTEM-task escalation (S-1-5-18 from a user-context install) is itself an anomaly worth raising. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/rvtools-masquerade-how-a-signed-fake-installer-deploys-a-modular-python-rat/107384
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
let RunKey = DeviceRegistryEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
    | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
    | where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\", "Pmanager.py", "collector.py")
    | where RegistryValueData has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","Pmanager.py","collector.py")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let SchedTask = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType in ("ScheduledTaskCreated","ScheduledTaskUpdated")
    | where AdditionalFields has_any ("Pmanager.py","collector.py")
        or (AdditionalFields has @"\AppData\" and AdditionalFields has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe"))
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName;
union RunKey, SchedTask
| order by Timestamp desc
let RunKey = ImRegistryEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
    | where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\", "Pmanager.py", "collector.py")
    | where RegistryValueData has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","Pmanager.py","collector.py")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName;
let SchedTask = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4698
    | where EventData has_any ("Pmanager.py","collector.py")
        or (EventData has @"\AppData\" and EventData has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe"))
    | extend RunsAsSystem = EventData has "S-1-5-18" or EventData has "NT AUTHORITY\\SYSTEM"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventData, RunsAsSystem;
union RunKey, SchedTask
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c1d8f4a7-6e92-4a05-8b3d-1f9e7c8b2d4a

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a") or SHA1 in~ ("d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a") or MD5 in~ ("d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a") or SHA1 in~ ("d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a") or MD5 in~ ("d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["d0f5e98fb840fb5656d3f50613b6f1ec60e57392643159841bc1fa95396087a4", "64bda120cb447e0c03f451190022a57b", "01a115c6f6ba3837234202a1e0d28bdc", "71085940124ad3c035a181acadc10362", "9192d18a955a9d03e2c70b60aac1784a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] smbd-descendant outbound connection to public IP (post-CVE-2026-4480 C2 / payload pull)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
[LLM] Samba smbd spawning shell or scripting interpreter (CVE-2026-4480 RCE) Exploitation High
Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-4480 in Samba's print subsystem: an attacker-controlled %J print-job description string is substituted into the configured 'print command' without shell-metacharacter escaping, causing smbd to spawn a shell or interpreter as a direct child. Under a healthy printing config (cups/iprint or a quoted %J) smbd should only invoke the configured print backend (lpr/lp/lpadmin), never sh/bash/python/perl/curl/wget. Rationale: Pivot is article-specific: CVE-2026-4480 is triggered when smbd substitutes %J into a 'print command' without escaping, and the immediate observable effect is smbd spawning a shell/interpreter (the injected command runs via sh -c). Under non-vulnerable configs (printing=cups/iprint, quoted '%J', or %J removed) smbd's print-time children are restricted to the print spool binary (lpr/lp/cupsd) — sh/bash/python/curl/wget/nc as a direct smbd child is the smoking gun. We did not externally cross-check this UC: CVE-2026-4480 is too recent to have public corroboration beyond the disclosing researchers (SafeBreach, ZeroPath, Securin Labs) named in the article and the Samba security page it points to.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "smbd"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","ash","python","python2","python3","perl","ruby","php","nc","ncat","socat","curl","wget","busybox","awk","gawk")
   or FolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or FolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/" or FolderPath startswith "/run/shm/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs has "linux" or DvcOs has "unix" or isempty(DvcOs)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/smbd" or ParentProcessName =~ "smbd"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ksh|ash|python[0-9]?|perl|ruby|php|nc|ncat|socat|curl|wget|busybox|awk|gawk)$"
   or ActingProcessName matches regex @"^/(tmp|var/tmp|dev/shm|run/shm)/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-4480 where Samba's smbd substitutes an unsanitized %J print-job description into the configured print command, causing smbd to spawn a shell or scripting interpreter as a child process. [LLM] smbd-descendant outbound connection to public IP (post-CVE-2026-4480 C2 / payload pull) Command & Control High
Detects the second-stage signal of CVE-2026-4480 exploitation: a process whose immediate parent is smbd makes an outbound connection to a public address. Catches reverse-shell call-backs and curl/wget payload retrieval initiated by the injected %J command even when the initial shell binary itself isn't on the UC1 watchlist (e.g. attacker uses 'python -c' directly as the print command's child, or a statically-linked dropper). Rationale: Distinct telemetry pivot (network egress + parent-process attribution) from UC1 (process spawn). Defender's DeviceNetworkEvents preserves InitiatingProcessParentFileName which makes the smbd-as-grandparent linkage trivially expressible; on Falcon we join NetworkConnectIP4 to ProcessRollup2 via aid+ContextProcessId to recover the same chain. Sentinel left empty — none of the ASIM tables in the schema (ImNetworkSession, Syslog, CommonSecurityLog) carry parent-process name on Linux network events without custom auditd parsing, so a reliable expression isn't possible on the documented schema. No external corroboration searched for this CVE specifically; the detection design follows generic post-exploit-egress patterns scoped to smbd as the unique parent.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "smbd"
| where RemoteIPType in ("Public","Internet")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          ParentBinary    = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ChildBinary     = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ChildCommand    = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
title: Outbound Network Connection From smbd Child Process (CVE-2026-4480 Post-Exploit)

description: Detects outbound network connections by a process whose parent is Samba's smbd, going to a non-RFC1918 destination. Catches the C2 callback or payload-pull stage of CVE-2026-4480 exploitation even when the spawned binary isn't on the standard shell/interpreter watchlist.

source:linux.auditd @process.parent.name:smbd @network.destination.ip:* -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 192.168.0.0/16) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 127.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 169.254.0.0/16)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4

| join(query={#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^smbd$/i | rename(field=TargetProcessId, as=ContextProcessId) | groupBy([aid, ContextProcessId, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId], include=[ImageFileName, CommandLine])

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-4480")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-4480")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData

OfficeActivity

| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Kimsuky fake AhnLab/nProtect installer spawning regsvr32 with MemLoader.dll Installation High
Detects the Kimsuky HTTPSpy installer chain where nos-setup.exe (fake nProtect Online Security) or astx-setup.exe (fake AhnLab Safe Transaction / ASTx) launches regsvr32.exe to side-load MemLoader.dll, the second-stage DLL that establishes scheduled-task persistence and beacons to C2. Rationale: Uses three article-specific strings together (parent binaries nos-setup.exe / astx-setup.exe + regsvr32 child + MemLoader.dll cmdline). All three named explicitly by ENKI as the Kimsuky HTTPSpy installer chain. Cross-checked against MITRE Kimsuky/G0094 and CrowdStrike's 2025 European Threat Landscape mention of HTTPSpy. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html
ATT&CKT1218.010 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nos-setup.exe","astx-setup.exe")
| where FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "MemLoader.dll" or ProcessCommandLine has "MemLoader"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\nos-setup.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\astx-setup.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
| where CommandLine has "MemLoader.dll" or CommandLine has "MemLoader"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Fake Webex camera-fix JSE dropper (fix-camera.jse) via wscript / mTSTCv8.mdxm Delivery High
Detects the April 2026 Kimsuky Webex lure where the victim runs an encrypted JScript file fix-camera.jse via wscript/cscript, which uses PowerShell to drop the intermediate downloader mTSTCv8.mdxm before fetching engine.dat / spyInster.dll. Hunts for either the JSE file execution or the unusual .mdxm extension on disk. Rationale: The .mdxm extension is a non-standard Kimsuky-specific artifact named in the ENKI report; fix-camera.jse and mTSTCv8.mdxm are unique enough that any hit is high-fidelity. Combines the JSE delivery vector with the intermediate-downloader filename. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/

[LLM] HTTPSpy loader-chain artifacts on disk (cacheMon.dat, engine.dat, spyInster.dll) Installation High
Detects creation of the unique Kimsuky HTTPSpy stage filenames - cacheMon.dat (loader), engine.dat / spyInster.dll (mid-stage DLLs), mTSTCv8.mdxm (intermediate downloader), MemLoader.dll (installer DLL), and fix-camera.jse - regardless of which entry vector dropped them. Rationale: These six filenames are HTTPSpy/Kimsuky-specific and unlikely to collide with anything benign (engine.dat is generic on its own but in combination with the other five becomes a strong cluster). Disk-write detection catches both the installer and Webex JSE chains in one rule. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html

[LLM] VS Code Remote Tunnel abuse for covert C2 (code tunnel) Command & Control Medium
Detects execution of Microsoft VS Code's Remote Tunneling feature (code.exe / code-tunnel.exe with the 'tunnel' subcommand) which Kaspersky observed Kimsuky abusing to establish covert C2 without traditional malware. Tunes for non-developer accounts on hosts that do not normally run VS Code. Rationale: Targets the specific 'code tunnel' invocation pattern Kaspersky documented as Kimsuky's TTP. Includes the --accept-server-license-terms / --random-name / serve-web args that distinguish the C2 use from a developer's normal VS Code launch. Also flagged by Darktrace and Logpresso per the article. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1219 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("code.exe","code-tunnel.exe","code-insiders.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--accept-server-license-terms","--name","--random-name","serve-web"," tunnel ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\code.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\code-tunnel.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\code-insiders.exe"
| where CommandLine has "tunnel"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--accept-server-license-terms","--name","--random-name","serve-web")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] AppleSeed GPKI directory enumeration / staging Actions on Objectives High
Detects access, copy, or read of files under C:\GPKI - the South Korean Government Public Key Infrastructure certificate directory that the AppleSeed Spy variant (and Troll Stealer before it) specifically targets per Kaspersky's 2026 Kimsuky report. Excludes platform processes that legitimately enumerate the filesystem. Rationale: C:\GPKI is specifically named in the article (Kaspersky / Troll Stealer mirror) as the AppleSeed exfil target. Korean GPKI certificates are tied to government / enterprise identity and have no benign reason to be touched by non-platform processes. Cross-referenced with prior Troll Stealer reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\GPKI\" or PreviousFolderPath has @"\GPKI\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","searchprotocolhost.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","sense.exe","sensesc.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "\\GPKI\\" or TargetFilePath has "/GPKI/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Kimsuky C2 callback to .r-e.kr / .o-r.kr / .n-e.kr dynamic-DNS infrastructure Command & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTPS callbacks to the Kimsuky 2026 campaign C2 set: eight explicit dynamic-DNS hostnames from ENKI plus the broader .r-e.kr / .o-r.kr / .n-e.kr TLD patterns the actor consistently uses. Both HTTPSpy and AppleSeed clusters use this infrastructure. Rationale: All eight FQDNs are ENKI-published Kimsuky 2026 C2 hosts. The .r-e.kr / .o-r.kr / .n-e.kr dynamic-DNS pattern is also documented as a Kimsuky staple by Kaspersky and CrowdStrike across multiple years, so the TLD-wide fallback catches future campaign rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (KimsukyDomains) or RemoteUrl endswith ".r-e.kr" or RemoteUrl endswith ".o-r.kr" or RemoteUrl endswith ".n-e.kr"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

( CommonSecurityLog

[LLM] MemLoader scheduled-task persistence after regsvr32 DLL load Installation Medium
Detects the Kimsuky MemLoader persistence step where, after regsvr32 loads MemLoader.dll, a schtasks /create is issued to re-launch the DLL (often referencing regsvr32, the MemLoader path, or AppData/Public stage paths). Article states 'DLL establishes persistence on the host using a scheduled task'. Rationale: schtasks /create alone is too noisy; combining it with the article's specific stage-binary names (MemLoader, cacheMon, spyInster) plus the user-writable AppData/Public stage paths anchors the detection to the Kimsuky chain. Parent exclusion drops admin GUI-driven task creation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("regsvr32","MemLoader","cacheMon","spyInster","\\AppData\\","\\Public\\",".dll")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("mmc.exe","taskschd.msc","trustedinstaller.exe","msiexec.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("regsvr32","MemLoader","cacheMon","spyInster","\\AppData\\","\\Public\\",".dll")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\mmc.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\TrustedInstaller.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SchTasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:*"/create"* @CommandLine:(*regsvr32* OR *MemLoader* OR *cacheMon* OR *spyInster* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Public\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\/create/i CommandLine=/(regsvr32|MemLoader|cacheMon|spyInster|\\AppData\\|\\Public\\)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
