Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to known infrastructure IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to known infrastructure IPs Command & Control High
Detects any corporate-network egress to the BTMOB RAT command-and-control IP set published by ESET and Cyble. BTMOB uses WebSocket-based C2 on these endpoints; a single connection from a managed Android (or any) device is high-fidelity since these IPs serve no legitimate enterprise purpose. Rationale: Direct IOC match against the 8 C2 IPs the article lists. Cross-checked with ESET WeLiveSecurity BTMOB write-up and Cyble's Feb-2025 BTMOB 2.5 analysis — same infrastructure cluster, WebSocket C2 protocol — so these IPs aren't fronting CDNs or shared hosting most enterprises would naturally touch. Defender for Endpoint covers Android too, so DeviceNetworkEvents surfaces the BYOD/MDM-enrolled phone egress as well as desktop hits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/ • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/btmob-android-rat-maas-builder/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1437.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
let BTMOB_C2 = dynamic(["78.135.93.123","79.133.57.141","178.156.177.192","191.101.131.250","195.160.221.203","191.96.224.87","191.96.225.241","191.96.78.172"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents

[LLM] BTMOB phishing/C2 domain lookup: arbsniper.com Delivery High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP/S contact with arbsniper.com, the clearnet front for the BTMOB malware-as-a-service identified by ESET. The domain hosts the operator portal and BTMOB lure infrastructure; any enterprise device touching it is either a victim of a phishing redirect or an operator/researcher pivot. Rationale: Single high-confidence domain published in the BleepingComputer article and confirmed as the BTMOB operator portal in ESET's WeLiveSecurity write-up. Domain is exclusive to the MaaS operation — no shared SaaS hosting risk. Covers DNS-layer hits (DnsEvents / ImDnsActivity), egress proxy hits, and Defender's UrlClickEvents so we catch a user clicking the phishing URL out of email as well as on-device beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/ • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/

[LLM] BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 observed on managed device Installation High
Detects file-write, download, or attachment events matching the 8 BTMOB SHA256 hashes published by ESET. Covers BYOD/MDM-enrolled Android endpoints, corporate Windows hosts that may have been used to sideload an APK to a phone via USB, and email attachment scanning. Rationale: Exact-hash IOC match — zero-FP by construction once cross-checked against an authoritative source. Hashes pulled straight from BleepingComputer / ESET write-up and corroborated against Cyble's BTMOB 2.5 sample set. Defender for Endpoint covers Android, so DeviceFileEvents picks up APK drops on enrolled phones; EmailAttachmentInfo covers the email-delivery vector; AlertEvidence catches AV/MDE detonation hits that already triggered. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/ • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://forum.eset.com/topic/49121-btmob-a-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-into-android-devices

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("78.135.93.123", "79.133.57.141", "178.156.177.192", "191.101.131.250", "195.160.221.203", "191.96.224.87", "191.96.225.241", "191.96.78.172", "191.96.78.28", "191.96.79.133", "191.96.79.179", "191.96.79.41", "200.9.155.153")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("arbsniper.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("arbsniper.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("78.135.93.123", "79.133.57.141", "178.156.177.192", "191.101.131.250", "195.160.221.203", "191.96.224.87", "191.96.225.241", "191.96.78.172", "191.96.78.28", "191.96.79.133", "191.96.79.179", "191.96.79.41", "200.9.155.153")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("arbsniper.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("arbsniper.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

FBI warns of fake FIFA websites running World Cup fraud schemes

BleepingComputer
2026-05-28 9 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The FBI is warning of fake websites impersonating FIFA ahead of the 2026 World Cup, to steal personal and financial information, sell fake tickets and hospitality packages, and push other fraud related to the event. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] DNS/HTTP traffic to Ghost Stadium FIFA typosquat domains (2026 World Cup fraud) · [LLM] Browser navigation to FIFA-themed look-alike hostname (typosquat pattern hunt) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Ghost Stadium FIFA fraud staging IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Risky AAD sign-in after user contact with FIFA typosquat phishing portal
[LLM] DNS/HTTP traffic to Ghost Stadium FIFA typosquat domains (2026 World Cup fraud) Delivery High
Hunts for endpoint resolution or HTTP requests to the eight FIFA look-alike domains called out in the FBI 2026 World Cup PSA and Group-IB's Ghost Stadium reporting. High-fidelity because these hostnames have no legitimate business use. Rationale: Uses the eight specific typosquat hostnames named by the FBI PSA and the Group-IB Ghost Stadium report. Hostnames have no legitimate business use; first-touch is high-fidelity for both DNS and proxy logs.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1189 T1583.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution
let TyposquatDomains = dynamic(["fiffa.com","jobs-fifa.com","fifa-hiring.com","filfa.org","wvvw-fifa.com","ww-fifa.com","fifa-hr.com","fifa-careerhub.com"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (TyposquatDomains)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, Source="DeviceNetworkEvents";
let ClickHits = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where Url has_any (TyposquatDomains)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName="", AccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName="", RemoteUrl=Url, RemoteIP="", Source="UrlClickEvents";
union NetHits, ClickHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let TyposquatDomains = dynamic(["fiffa.com","jobs-fifa.com","fifa-hiring.com","filfa.org","wvvw-fifa.com","ww-fifa.com","fifa-hr.com","fifa-careerhub.com"]);
union
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where Name has_any (TyposquatDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Host=Name, Source="DNS"),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where RequestURL has_any (TyposquatDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (TyposquatDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Host=coalesce(DestinationHostName,RequestURL), Source="Proxy"),
(W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where csReferer has_any (TyposquatDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, Host=csReferer, Source="IIS-Referer")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FIFA Typosquat Domain Lookup (Ghost Stadium 2026 World Cup Fraud)
id: 7a4b9e6e-1c2f-4b9d-8e5a-d4d2f5e3b6a1
description: Detects DNS resolution or HTTP traffic to FIFA typosquat domains associated with the FBI 2026 World Cup PSA and Group-IB's Ghost Stadium campaign.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-of-fake-fifa-websites-running-world-cup-fraud-schemes/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1189
  - attack.t1583.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains:
      - 'fiffa.com'
      - 'jobs-fifa.com'
      - 'fifa-hiring.com'
      - 'filfa.org'
      - 'wvvw-fifa.com'
      - 'ww-fifa.com'
      - 'fifa-hr.com'
      - 'fifa-careerhub.com'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Threat-intel analysts pivoting on IOCs
  - Email-security sandbox detonation
level: high
(@network.destination.domain:(fiffa.com OR jobs-fifa.com OR fifa-hiring.com OR filfa.org OR wvvw-fifa.com OR ww-fifa.com OR fifa-hr.com OR fifa-careerhub.com) OR @http.url_details.host:(fiffa.com OR jobs-fifa.com OR fifa-hiring.com OR filfa.org OR wvvw-fifa.com OR ww-fifa.com OR fifa-hr.com OR fifa-careerhub.com) OR @dns.question.name:(fiffa.com OR jobs-fifa.com OR fifa-hiring.com OR filfa.org OR wvvw-fifa.com OR ww-fifa.com OR fifa-hr.com OR fifa-careerhub.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^(fiffa\.com|jobs-fifa\.com|fifa-hiring\.com|filfa\.org|wvvw-fifa\.com|ww-fifa\.com|fifa-hr\.com|fifa-careerhub\.com)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

[LLM] Outbound connection to Ghost Stadium FIFA fraud staging IPs Command & Control High
Alerts when any internal host establishes an outbound connection to the eight staging IPs that host the cloned FIFA ticketing/employment/merchandise portals. Catches cases where the typosquat domain was bypassed via direct link, URL shortener, or DNS-over-HTTPS resolution that escaped DNS-tier visibility. Rationale: Targets the eight staging IPs explicitly pre-extracted from the FBI PSA / Group-IB infrastructure tracking. IP-tier detection catches victims who reach the cloned portals via shortened URLs or DoH that bypass DNS visibility.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
let StagingIPs = dynamic(["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (StagingIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let StagingIPs = dynamic(["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (StagingIPs) or SourceIP in (StagingIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to Ghost Stadium FIFA Fraud Staging IPs

detection:

      - '148.178.18.23'
      - '148.178.18.60'
      - '154.86.0.33'
      - '207.56.1.93'
      - '66.112.212.25'
      - '148.178.16.48'
      - '148.178.16.5'
      - '104.225.235.49'
  condition: selection

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(148\.178\.18\.23|148\.178\.18\.60|154\.86\.0\.33|207\.56\.1\.93|66\.112\.212\.25|148\.178\.16\.48|148\.178\.16\.5|104\.225\.235\.49)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs

| filter dstAddr in ["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]

[LLM] Browser navigation to FIFA-themed look-alike hostname (typosquat pattern hunt) Delivery Medium
Hunting query that surfaces browser traffic to any domain matching the FIFA typosquat pattern family (extra/missing letters, hyphenated subbrands like -hiring/-hr/-careerhub/-ticket, doubled-W prefixes) excluding the legitimate fifa.com/fifa.org. Designed to catch the long tail of the 300+ Ghost Stadium domains beyond the eight in the FBI PSA. Rationale: Article + Group-IB attribution names 300+ Ghost Stadium domains, only 8 of which are pre-extracted. The regex covers the family of typosquat patterns described (homoglyph: fiffa/filfa/f1fa, doubled-W: wvvw-/ww-, sub-brand hyphens: -hiring/-hr/-ticket/-careerhub) while explicitly excluding genuine fifa.com/fifa.org.

[LLM] Risky AAD sign-in after user contact with FIFA typosquat phishing portal Actions on Objectives Medium
Correlates users who visited any of the Ghost Stadium FIFA typosquat domains with subsequent risky/anomalous Entra ID sign-ins within 7 days. Targets the post-credential-submission account-takeover pivot described in the article ('create fraudulent accounts, commit identity theft'). Rationale: The article explicitly states the harvested PII/credentials are used 'to create fraudulent accounts, commit identity theft'. Joining typosquat visitors against subsequent risky AAD sign-ins is the only way to spot the account-takeover step. The 7-day delay window covers actor lag between data collection and credential reuse.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or SHA1 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or MD5 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or SHA1 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or MD5 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hackers Use LLM Agent to Move From Marimo RCE to Internal Database in Four Pivots

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new kind of cyberattack is changing how defenders must think about intrusion detection. On May 10, 2026, a threat actor used a large language model (LLM) agent to drive a full post-exploitation chain, starting from an exposed notebook server and ending with an internal database dumped in under two minutes. This was not a [&#8230;] The post Hackers Use LLM Agent to Move From Marimo RCE to Internal Database in Four Pivots appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] marimo notebook Python process spawning interactive shell (CVE-2026-39987 post-exploit) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Burst AWS API calls fanned across Cloudflare Workers egress (104.28.0.0/16) for one principal · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS Secrets Manager retrieval from Cloudflare Workers egress pool · [LLM] SSH authentication to bastion from Cloudflare Workers CIDR (104.28.0.0/16) · [LLM] PostgreSQL HEREDOC credential-table dump invoked from compromised host
[LLM] marimo notebook Python process spawning interactive shell (CVE-2026-39987 post-exploit) Exploitation High
Detects post-exploitation of CVE-2026-39987 where the marimo notebook server's Python process spawns an interactive shell via the abused /terminal/ws WebSocket endpoint. The shell child of a marimo-bearing Python parent is the on-host fingerprint of the one-WebSocket-request RCE Sysdig documented. Rationale: Article names marimo + CVE-2026-39987 + /terminal/ws as the entry. On-host the abused terminal feature surfaces as a Python(marimo) → bash child; pairing that parent with the credential-file enumeration strings (.aws/credentials, .pgpass) the article calls out makes this fire on the actual intrusion shape, not generic Python-spawns-shell noise.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("id","whoami","/.aws/credentials","/.pgpass","env","find /","ls /")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "marimo"
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("id","whoami","/.aws/credentials","/.pgpass","env","find /")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
title: marimo Notebook Python Process Spawning Interactive Shell (CVE-2026-39987)
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-4789-abcd-ef1234567890
description: Detects post-exploitation shell spawn from a marimo notebook server, the on-host fingerprint of CVE-2026-39987 /terminal/ws WebSocket RCE.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(python|python3|uvicorn)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|dash|zsh)$/i
| CommandLine=/(marimo|\.aws\/credentials|\.pgpass|whoami|find\s+\/)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

[LLM] Burst AWS API calls fanned across Cloudflare Workers egress (104.28.0.0/16) for one principal Command & Control High
Detects the LLM-agent evasion fingerprint Sysdig described: 10+ AWS API calls from one IAM principal/role within a sub-minute window, originating from many distinct IPs inside the Cloudflare Workers CIDR. This breaks per-source-IP correlation and is unlike legitimate Cloudflare-Workers-backed workloads which typically use a stable role and steady cadence. Rationale: Article: 12 AWS API calls fanned across 11 distinct Cloudflare Workers IPs in 22 seconds for the same principal. The 5-distinct-IPs-and-10-calls-in-2-minutes shape directly mirrors that burst while staying comfortably above any single-app Cloudflare-Workers usage pattern. CIDR + same-principal aggregation is the key — neither alone is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
source:cloudtrail CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.0.0/16) NOT @userIdentity.type:AWSService
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName
| filter sourceIPAddress like /^104\.28\./
      and userIdentity.type != "AWSService"
| stats count(*) as api_calls, count_distinct(sourceIPAddress) as src_ips, count_distinct(eventName) as distinct_apis, latest(eventName) as last_event by userIdentity.arn, bin(2m)
| filter api_calls >= 10 and src_ips >= 5
| sort api_calls desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, _time span=2m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as distinct_src_ips, dc(action) as distinct_actions, sum(count) as api_calls, values(src) as src_ips, values(action) as actions by user, _time | where distinct_src_ips >= 5 AND api_calls >= 10
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, _time span=2m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as distinct_src_ips, dc(action) as distinct_actions, sum(count) as api_calls, values(src) as src_ips, values(action) as actions by user, _time | where distinct_src_ips >= 5 AND api_calls >= 10
[LLM] AWS Secrets Manager retrieval from Cloudflare Workers egress pool Actions on Objectives High
Detects ListSecrets / GetSecretValue CloudTrail events originating from the 104.28.0.0/16 Cloudflare Workers CIDR. In the Sysdig intrusion this exact pair retrieved the SSH private key the agent used to pivot to the bastion — the source-IP-vs-Secrets-Manager combination is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article: AWS Secrets Manager call retrieved an SSH private key, source IP 104.28.0.0/16. Pairing eventSource secretsmanager.amazonaws.com with the Cloudflare Workers CIDR is the article's exact fingerprint — sub-second decision, single CloudTrail line.
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1555.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
title: AWS Secrets Manager Retrieval From Cloudflare Workers Egress Pool
id: b2c3d4e5-f6a7-4801-bcde-f23456789012
description: Detects AWS Secrets Manager retrieval calls originating from the 104.28.0.0/16 Cloudflare Workers CIDR used by the LLM-agent intrusion to grab an SSH key.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-llm-agent-to-move-from-marimo-rce/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.006
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: 'secretsmanager.amazonaws.com'
    eventName:
      - 'GetSecretValue'
      - 'ListSecrets'
    sourceIPAddress|startswith: '104.28.'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Customer-owned Cloudflare Worker that legitimately retrieves secrets via the AWS SDK (allowlist by principal ARN)
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(GetSecretValue OR ListSecrets) CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.0.0/16)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail

[LLM] SSH authentication to bastion from Cloudflare Workers CIDR (104.28.0.0/16) Actions on Objectives High
Detects successful SSH logons originating from the Cloudflare Workers egress pool, with multi-IP parallelism per user — the bastion-pivot stage Sysdig observed where eight parallel SSH sessions originated from six distinct CF Workers IPs against the same downstream bastion. Internal users virtually never authenticate to bastions via Cloudflare's CDN range. Rationale: Article: 8 SSH sessions came from 6 separate CF Workers IPs simultaneously against the bastion. Joining "successful sshd Accepted" with "src in 104.28.0.0/16" + the multi-IP-per-user aggregation hits the actual fan-out shape, not a generic CDN-IP false positive.
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1090.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where Protocol == "Ssh" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sshd"
| where ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "104.28.0.0/16")
| summarize SessionCount = count(), SrcIPs = make_set(RemoteIP), DistinctSrc = dcount(RemoteIP), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctSrc >= 3 or SessionCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName =~ "sshd"
| where SyslogMessage has "Accepted"
| extend SrcIP = extract(@"from\s+(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage), SshUser = extract(@"for\s+(\S+)\s+from", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where SrcIP startswith "104.28."
| summarize SessionCount = count(), SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIP), DistinctSrc = dcount(SrcIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, SshUser, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSrc >= 3 or SessionCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:sshd "Accepted" CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.0.0/16)
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^104\.28\./
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function={count() | distinct_count(RemoteAddressIP4, as=distinct_src) | min(_time, as=firstSeen) | max(_time, as=lastSeen)})
| distinct_src >= 3 OR _count >= 5
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action, bytes
| filter dstPort = 22 and action = "ACCEPT"
      and srcAddr like /^104\.28\./
| stats count(*) as flows, count_distinct(srcAddr) as src_ips, sum(bytes) as bytes_sent by dstAddr, bin(10m)
| filter src_ips >= 3 or flows >= 5
| sort @timestamp desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=sshd Authentication.action=success by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, Authentication.dest, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as src_count sum(count) as session_count values(src) as src_ips by user, dest, bin_time | where src_count >= 3 OR session_count >= 5
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=sshd Authentication.action=success by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, Authentication.dest, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as src_count sum(count) as session_count values(src) as src_ips by user, dest, bin_time | where src_count >= 3 OR session_count >= 5
[LLM] PostgreSQL HEREDOC credential-table dump invoked from compromised host Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects psql being invoked with a HEREDOC and credential-table-targeting queries (users, credentials, password columns), often immediately preceded by a .pgpass read by the same user — the database exfiltration pattern Sysdig captured when the LLM agent enumerated the schema and immediately dumped a credential table that didn't even belong to the running application. Rationale: Article: agent read .pgpass, enumerated schema, and immediately dumped a credential table that doesn't belong to the running app, using HEREDOC-style structured commands. psql + (credential-table keywords OR `<<EOF` OR `COPY (`) is the article-specific intent; cross-correlating with a .pgpass read by the same account in the same window further sharpens it.
ATT&CKT1005 T1213 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let PgpassReaders = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName == ".pgpass" or FolderPath endswith "/.pgpass"
    | where ActionType in ("FileOpenedForRead","FileCreated","FileModified")
    | project PgpassTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("psql","pg_dump")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"<<\s*[A-Z_]+"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select"
| join kind=leftouter PgpassReaders on DeviceId, $left.AccountName == $right.InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where isnotempty(PgpassTime) or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("credentials","users","<<")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, PgpassTime
| order by Timestamp desc
let PgpassReaders = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetFileName == ".pgpass" or TargetFilePath endswith "/.pgpass"
    | project PgpassTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("psql","pg_dump")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"<<\s*[A-Z_]+"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select"
| join kind=leftouter PgpassReaders on DvcHostname, $left.ActorUsername == $right.ActorUsername
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, PgpassTime
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PostgreSQL Credential Table Dump via psql HEREDOC
id: c3d4e5f6-a7b8-4923-cdef-345678901234
description: Detects psql/pg_dump invocations consuming a HEREDOC and targeting credential or user tables — the database exfiltration step the LLM-agent intrusion executed against an internal PostgreSQL.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-llm-agent-to-move-from-marimo-rce/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1005
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1213
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/psql'
      - '/pg_dump'
  selection_intent:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'credentials'
      - 'users'
      - 'password'
      - 'secrets'
      - 'api_keys'
      - 'tokens'
      - '<<EOF'
      - 'COPY ('
  condition: selection_proc and selection_intent
falsepositives:
  - Application owners running ad-hoc COPY/SELECT against legitimate user tables
  - Backup jobs invoking pg_dump
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(psql OR pg_dump) @process.command_line:(*credentials* OR *password* OR *users* OR *secrets* OR *api_keys* OR *"<<EOF"* OR *"COPY ("*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(psql|pg_dump)$/i
| CommandLine=/(credentials|password|users|secrets|api_keys|tokens|<<\s*EOF|COPY\s*\()/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("psql","pg_dump") by host, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)") OR match(process,"<<\s*[A-Z_]+") OR match(process,"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select") | join type=left host, user [| tstats summariesonly=true count as pgpass_reads from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".pgpass" by host, Filesystem.user | rename Filesystem.user as user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`] | table _time host user process parent_process_name pgpass_reads
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("psql","pg_dump") by host, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)") OR match(process,"<<\s*[A-Z_]+") OR match(process,"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select") | join type=left host, user [| tstats summariesonly=false count as pgpass_reads from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".pgpass" by host, Filesystem.user | rename Filesystem.user as user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`] | table _time host user process parent_process_name pgpass_reads
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39987")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39987")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Less panic patching, more precision
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VaultJacking Attack Steals Entire Google Password Manager Vault With One Captured PIN

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new phishing technique called VaultJacking has emerged, and it is raising serious alarms across the cybersecurity community. With just a single captured 6-digit PIN, an attacker can walk away with an entire Google Password Manager vault, including every saved password and passkey stored inside. This is not a theoretical risk, as it is a [&#8230;] The post VaultJacking Attack Steals Entire Google Password Manager Vault With One Captured PIN appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Browser navigation to Google Password Manager PIN prompt lookalike domain (VaultJacking phishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New Google passkey / security key enrolled from unseen geo or IP (VaultJacking operator persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Browser navigation to Google Password Manager PIN prompt lookalike domain (VaultJacking phishing) Delivery Medium
Hunts the phishing prerequisite for VaultJacking: a user's browser visiting a non-google.com host that impersonates passwords.google.com / the GPM PIN prompt. VaultJacking is uniquely keyed on the 6-digit GPM PIN, so the phishing page mimics passwords.google.com / passkey-unlock surfaces rather than the standard accounts.google.com sign-in page — this is the differentiator from generic Google credential phishing. Rationale: Article (and corroborating gbhackers writeup) state the phishing page specifically mimics the Google Password Manager PIN prompt at passwords.google.com — a unique surface from generic accounts.google.com phishing. Hunting URL/hostname tokens that combine 'google' (or g00gle) with 'passwords'/'passkey'/'gpm'/'vault' targets the VaultJacking lure category specifically while excluding legitimate google.com traffic. Cross-checked: cybersecuritynews and gbhackers articles, MITRE T1566.002 / T1598.003. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/google-password-vaults-via-single-pin/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| extend UrlLower = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where Host !endswith ".google.com" and Host != "google.com"
| where UrlLower has_any ("passwords-google","google-passwords","googlepasswords",
                          "passkey-google","google-passkey","googlepasskey",
                          "gpm-pin","gpm-google","google-gpm",
                          "vault-google","google-vault")
   or Host matches regex @"(?i)g[o0]{2}gle.*(passw|passk|gpm)"
   or Host matches regex @"(?i)(passw|passk|gpm)[^.]*g[o0]{2}gle"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          BrowserProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName,
          RemoteUrl, Host, RemoteIP,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
